chapters.title: Chapter 4: Dilution, Down Rounds and Protecting Your Stake

lessons.title: Tracking Dilution From Seed to Series C

children.text: You have now seen dilution one round at a time. The question that matters for your returns is different: after three, four or five rounds, how much of your original stake is left, and what is it worth? Many first-time angels assume their 1.25% stays roughly 1.25%. It rarely does. This lesson gives you one simple multiplication to project your stake through any number of rounds, and shows why an angel can own half as much of a company and still be far richer on paper.

body.text: Dilution compounds. Each round keeps a fraction of your stake, and those fractions multiply. Your ownership shrinks round after round, but if each round is priced higher, the value of what remains can grow many times over.

children.text: In every round, existing holders are diluted by the new investor's stake plus any ESOP pool top-up created in the pre-money. What they keep is the

markDefs.definition: The fraction of an existing holder's ownership that survives a funding round: 1 minus the dilution from new shares issued.

body.latex: \text{Retention ratio} = 1 - \text{New investor's stake} - \text{New pool created in the pre-money}
body.caption: Both measured as a percentage of post-round capital

body.latex: \text{Stake after } n \text{ rounds} = \text{Starting stake} \times R_1 \times R_2 \times \cdots \times R_n
body.caption: Multiply the retention ratios. Never subtract the dilution percentages.

body.title: Why you must multiply, not subtract

children.text: Suppose three rounds dilute existing holders by 25%, 21% and 15%. It is tempting to add those up to 61% and conclude you keep 39% of your stake. That is wrong.
Each round dilutes what is left after the previous round, not your original stake. Subtracting overstates dilution, and the error grows with every round you add.

MachhBazaar Technologies Private Limited is a fictional Kolkata startup running a fresh fish delivery app that sources directly from wholesale markets. Kavya, a Kolkata-based doctor, invests ₹10 lakh in its seed round at an ₹8 crore post-money valuation, giving her 1.25%.

body.caption: Kavya's stake from seed to Series C (illustrative)

body.title: Kavya's stake: ownership falls, value rises
body.yAxisLabel: Paper value of her stake (₹ lakh)

body.text: Kavya's stake value rose because MachhBazaar's price per share rose at every round. Dilution only hurts in rupee terms when the new round is priced below the last one, which is a down round and the subject of the next lesson. Rising valuations do not make dilution disappear, they make it worth accepting.

This is still paper value. It assumes the Series C price holds until an exit, that no preferences sit ahead of Kavya's shares in a sale, and that the company eventually sells or lists. Chapter 5 shows how headline valuations and real payouts can differ.

body.title: Project a stake
body.prompt: You own 1% of a startup after its seed round. The next three rounds dilute existing holders by 20%, 20% and 15%. What is your ownership after the third round? Answer as a percentage to three decimal places.
body.explanation: Retention ratios are 0.80, 0.80 and 0.85. 1% × 0.80 × 0.80 × 0.85 = 0.544%. Subtracting instead would give 1% × (1 − 0.55) = 0.45%, understating what you keep.

children.text: The same multiplication applies to founders. Suppose MachhBazaar's founders owned 70% after the seed round, which included a new ESOP pool.

At 35% after Series C, the founders no longer control special resolutions on their own, and any further rounds will push them lower. This is normal for venture-funded companies, and it is exactly why founder control rights are negotiated so hard in later term sheets.

body.label: Two founders, two very different outcomes
body.context: Deepinder Goyal reportedly held around 5% of Zomato (now Eternal) around its 2021 IPO, after many rounds of venture funding. At Nykaa's IPO the same year, Falguni Nayar and her family held roughly half of its parent company, which had raised far less outside capital. How much you raise, and at what prices, decides how much you keep.

children.text: You cannot predict future rounds exactly, but you can use common ranges to build a realistic projection. These are broad market norms, not rules, and a strong company in a hot market will often dilute less.

body.caption: Common dilution ranges per round (new investor plus any pool top-up)

body.title: Spot the error
body.question: An angel says: "The next three rounds will dilute us by 25%, 20% and 15%. That is 60% in total, so I will keep 40% of my stake." What is wrong?
options: Dilution should be multiplied as retention ratios, giving 51% retained
Dilution should be averaged, giving 20% retained
The angel should divide by the number of rounds
body.explanation: 0.75 × 0.80 × 0.85 = 0.51, so the angel keeps 51% of their stake, not 40%. Each round dilutes the stake left after the previous round, so the percentages compound rather than add.

body.title: Name the fraction
body.textWithBlank: The fraction of your ownership that survives a funding round, calculated as 1 minus the dilution, is called the ___ ratio.
body.explanation: Multiplying retention ratios across rounds gives your cumulative retention. It is the same idea you met in the VC method in Lesson 2.3.

children.text: , where the new investor buys existing shares from early holders. Secondary sales do not create new shares, so they do not dilute anyone. They simply move ownership from one holder to another and give early angels or employees a chance to take some money off the table.

markDefs.definition: Part of a funding round in which a new investor buys existing shares from current holders, so the money goes to those sellers rather than to the company.

body.text: For an angel, selling even 20% to 30% of a stake in a strong Series B or C secondary can return your entire original cheque, leaving the rest as a free ride. Whether that beats holding on depends on how much you believe in the next few years, but it is worth asking whether a secondary is available when a big round is announced.

body.title: "Your 2% will still be 1.5% at IPO"
body.scenario: A Gurugram fintech founder pitches you at seed: "Put in ₹20 lakh for 2%. We plan to go public in about seven years, and you will still hold around 1.5% at IPO." Their plan shows a Series A, B, C and D before the IPO.
body.prompt: Test the claim using typical dilution ranges. What stake is more realistic at IPO?
body.modelAnswer:
To keep 1.5% of an original 2%, total retention must be 1.5 ÷ 2 = 75%. That means just 25% cumulative dilution across four rounds plus an IPO, which is very unlikely.

A more realistic path using mid-range assumptions:
1. Series A retention 0.75 (25% dilution including a pool top-up)
2. Series B retention 0.80
3. Series C retention 0.85
4. Series D retention 0.88
5. IPO fresh issue retention 0.90

2% × 0.75 × 0.80 × 0.85 × 0.88 × 0.90 = 0.81%.

A realistic expectation is roughly 0.8% to 1% at IPO, not 1.5%. That does not make it a bad investment, since the value could still rise sharply, but you should decide based on realistic ownership, and you may want pro-rata rights (Lesson 4.3) if staying above 1% matters to you.

body.title: Track dilution in your own angel portfolio
steps: Keep a simple sheet per startup: shares held, starting stake, and price paid.
For every new round, record the price per share, new shares issued and any pool top-up.
Update your stake by dividing your shares by the new fully diluted total, and check it against your retention ratio.
Update paper value as your shares multiplied by the latest round price, marked clearly as paper value.
Ask the company for the post-round cap table or PAS-3 filing after every round.
Note whether a secondary sale is offered, and whether you have pro-rata rights in the next round.

Your shares multiplied by the latest round price. Not cash until an exit or secondary sale.

points: Retention ratio = 1 minus the new investor's stake minus any pool top-up created in the pre-money.
Multiply retention ratios across rounds. Adding up dilution percentages gives the wrong answer.
A seed stake often roughly halves by Series C, and can fall well below half by IPO.
Ownership can fall while value rises, as long as each round is priced higher than the last.
Use typical dilution ranges to stress-test any founder claim about your future ownership.
Secondary sales move ownership without diluting anyone, and can let early angels recover their original cheque.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. MachhBazaar and the other startups and investors described are fictional, and the dilution ranges shown are broad market norms, not predictions. Figures for Zomato and Nykaa are approximate and based on public reports. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
